## In one minute

150 short, actionable tips (151-300 of 300) on debugging live failures, behavioural and ownership answers, common interview traps, communication and staff-level signals, and the interview day itself. They're written to be skimmed: about 12 seconds each. **Budget: 30 minutes.** Don't try to memorise them all: copy the ten that hit your weak spots onto one page and re-read that page in the final review.

## How to use these tips

- Skim a section, and when a tip makes you think "I wouldn't have said that", copy it.
- Turn each copied tip into a one-sentence habit ("In every design, I say what happens on a timeout").
- Practise the habit once aloud in a mock answer today.

## Tips 151-300

### Debugging live failures

151. Lead with mitigation in any incident answer: roll back, fail over, disable the flag, shed load; investigate after customers are safe.
152. Start from symptoms and SLIs (error rate, latency, success rate), then narrow down with traces, logs and metrics.
153. Ask "what changed?" first: deploys, configuration, traffic, dependencies, data.
154. Correlate the start of the problem with deploy and config-change timelines.
155. Take three thread dumps a few seconds apart; what persists across them is the real problem.
156. Many threads waiting on a connection pool means exhaustion; find what holds connections (slow queries, remote calls inside transactions).
157. High latency with low CPU usually means waiting: locks, pools, slow dependencies, missing timeouts.
158. High CPU: profile with async-profiler for 30 seconds and read the flame graph before guessing.
159. Rising old-generation usage after each GC over hours suggests a leak; confirm with heap dumps taken apart in time.
160. OOM-killed containers with a healthy heap point to non-heap memory; check Native Memory Tracking.
161. Latency spikes that don't match GC pauses: check CPU throttling, safepoints and downstream latency.
162. For database slowness, check `pg_stat_activity` for blocking, `pg_stat_statements` for top queries, and EXPLAIN plans.
163. Growing Kafka consumer lag: check for a poison message, a slow dependency in the consumer, rebalances or a hot partition.
164. A sudden rise in duplicates: look for retries without idempotency, consumer rebalances, or an outbox relay restart.
165. Payments stuck in UNKNOWN: check the PSP's status, the inquiry job, and network errors to the provider.
166. Reconciliation breaks spiking after a release: compare event schemas, rounding and timing changes in the new version.
167. Distinguish "the dependency is down" from "the dependency is slow"; slow is usually worse because it holds resources.
168. Check whether the problem is in one instance, one zone or everywhere; that tells you whether it's local or systemic.
169. Use feature flags to turn off a suspected feature quickly instead of redeploying.
170. Communicate status on a fixed rhythm during an incident, even when there's no news.
171. Write a timeline as you go; reconstructing it later is unreliable.
172. After recovery, verify with business metrics (payments succeeding), not just green dashboards.
173. Look for the lucky factors in a post-incident review; luck is a hidden risk.
174. Every incident should produce at least one test or alert that would have caught it earlier.
175. When you can't reproduce a production bug, add targeted logging or tracing and wait for the next occurrence rather than guessing.
176. Check clocks and time zones when date-related bugs appear around midnight, month ends or DST changes.
177. For intermittent failures, look for a resource limit: file descriptors, ephemeral ports, connection pools, thread caps.
178. Never debug by restarting everything repeatedly; capture evidence (dumps, logs) before restarting.
179. Keep heap dumps and logs secure; they contain customer data.
180. In interviews, narrate your hypothesis, the evidence that confirmed or rejected it, and the next step.

### Behavioural and ownership

181. Prepare six true STAR stories: an incident, a correctness bug, a disagreement, an ambiguous project, mentoring, and a mistake.
182. Keep each story to about two minutes; most of the time goes on your actions.
183. Use "I" for your actions and "we" only for team outcomes.
184. Include one concrete technical detail per action step; it's what makes a senior story credible.
185. End each story with a lasting change: a test, an alert, a runbook, a process.
186. Quantify results only with real numbers; "fewer pages after that" beats an invented percentage.
187. For "tell me about a failure", pick a real mistake, own it, and explain the guardrail that now prevents it.
188. For conflict questions, describe the other person's position fairly and how you decided on evidence.
189. Show "disagree and commit": you raised concerns, a decision was made, and you supported it fully.
190. For ambiguity questions, describe how you clarified the goal, made assumptions explicit and delivered in increments.
191. For mentoring, describe what the other person achieved, not how clever you were.
192. For ownership, show you followed a problem beyond your team's boundary until it was solved.
193. Show you communicate risk early: "I flagged it two weeks before the deadline with options."
194. Avoid blaming individuals, teams or vendors; describe systems and decisions.
195. Have a 60–90 second "tell me about yourself" that ends with why this role is the next step.
196. Prepare an answer for "why are you leaving?" that's positive and forward-looking.
197. Prepare an answer for "why this company?" tied to its product, domain or engineering challenges.
198. For staff-level roles, include a story about influencing a decision across several teams.
199. Include a story where you made something simpler or removed work; it shows judgement.
200. Include a story about improving reliability or developer experience with measurable effect.
201. Practise stories aloud and record yourself; written stories sound different when spoken.
202. If you lack a big story for a theme, use a smaller true one rather than inventing.
203. Expect follow-ups ("what would you do differently?"); prepare one for each story.
204. Show learning: what you now do differently because of the experience.
205. Mention how you kept stakeholders informed in incident and project stories.
206. For leadership without authority, mention RFCs, prototypes, data and sponsors.
207. Don't speak negatively about previous employers; interviewers project it onto themselves.
208. Show you care about customers' money and trust; in fintech it's a core value.
209. Be honest about what you don't know; curiosity scores better than bluffing.
210. Close behavioural rounds by asking a thoughtful question about the team's challenges.

### Common interview traps

211. Trap: "Use Kafka, so it's exactly-once." Answer with idempotent consumers and the outbox instead.
212. Trap: marking a timed-out payment as failed. Say UNKNOWN and explain resolution.
213. Trap: a distributed lock as the guarantee against double spending. Use database constraints or fencing.
214. Trap: `double` for money. Never.
215. Trap: "we'll add a cache" for a correctness problem. Caches add staleness, not consistency.
216. Trap: 2PC across microservices as the default. Prefer sagas and reconciliation, and explain why.
217. Trap: OFFSET pagination for large datasets. Use keyset pagination.
218. Trap: `FetchType.EAGER` as the N+1 fix. Use fetch joins or projections.
219. Trap: H2 for database tests. Use Testcontainers with the real engine.
220. Trap: liveness probes that check the database. Use readiness for dependencies.
221. Trap: retries at every layer. Retry at one layer with budgets and jitter.
222. Trap: no timeouts on HTTP clients. Always set connect and read timeouts.
223. Trap: putting a remote call inside a `@Transactional` method. Split into intent, call, result.
224. Trap: assuming `@Transactional` works on self-invocation or private methods.
225. Trap: "virtual threads make everything faster." They raise concurrency; limits move downstream.
226. Trap: parallel streams in a web service. They share the common pool.
227. Trap: `volatile` for compound updates. Use atomics or locks.
228. Trap: `synchronized` on a singleton service method that calls the database. It serialises everything and doesn't protect other instances.
229. Trap: ordering events by wall-clock time across machines. Use sequence numbers or partition order.
230. Trap: increasing Kafka partitions casually on a keyed topic. It remaps keys.
231. Trap: "eventual consistency is fine" for balance checks. Not for spending decisions.
232. Trap: forgetting authorisation on object ids (BOLA). Scope queries to the owner.
233. Trap: logging full requests with card numbers or personal data.
234. Trap: storing secrets in configuration files or Git.
235. Trap: claiming exact throughput numbers for a database from memory. Say you'd measure.
236. Trap: designing for the happy path only. Volunteer the failure path.
237. Trap: jumping into code without clarifying requirements and edge cases.
238. Trap: going silent while thinking. Narrate your reasoning.
239. Trap: defending a weak answer instead of correcting it. Saying "let me revise that" is a strength.
240. Trap: running out of time before the deep dive or before testing your code. Watch the clock.

### Communication and staff-level signals

241. Structure answers: headline first, then reasoning, then detail if asked.
242. Use precise words: linearizable, idempotent, at-least-once, serializable. Then explain them simply.
243. Check in with the interviewer every few minutes: "Is this the level of detail you want?"
244. When asked an open question, give a framework, then go deep on one part.
245. Admit uncertainty with a plan: "I'm not sure of the default; I'd verify, but the design doesn't depend on it."
246. Connect technical choices to business outcomes: money lost, customers affected, regulatory risk, cost.
247. Mention operability: how the system is deployed, monitored, debugged and rolled back.
248. Mention the team: who owns what, how decisions are made and documented.
249. Show you think about migration and coexistence, not only the target state.
250. Talk about risks and how you'd reduce them: prototypes, load tests, staged rollouts.
251. Be explicit about what you'd do first, second and third; prioritisation is a staff signal.
252. Show you can say no or "not yet" with reasons.
253. Refer to real experience briefly ("in a previous system we saw this exact failure") without long war stories.
254. Draw before you talk through complex flows; a sequence diagram saves minutes.
255. Summarise at natural breakpoints so the interviewer can follow and redirect.
256. Ask clarifying questions that change the design, not ones that stall it.
257. Use the interviewer's terminology once they introduce it.
258. When challenged, acknowledge the point, then reason about it; don't get defensive.
259. Show breadth with one sentence and depth with a paragraph; don't spend depth on everything.
260. Avoid buzzword stacking; each technology you name should have a reason.
261. Quantify where you can: latency budgets, volumes, error rates, costs.
262. Use analogies sparingly and only to clarify, not to replace precision.
263. In leadership questions, show how you grow other engineers and raise the team's standards.
264. In architecture discussions, mention standards and paved roads that help many teams, not just one system.
265. Talk about documentation (RFCs, ADRs, runbooks) as engineering tools, not bureaucracy.
266. Show you consider security and compliance as design inputs from the start.
267. Show cost awareness: what the design costs to run and how it scales with traffic.
268. Show you can simplify: remove a component, merge services, delete code.
269. End each round with a short recap of the key decisions and open questions.
270. Thank the interviewer and keep your energy consistent across rounds; each interviewer scores independently.

### Before and during the interview day

271. Re-read the job description and map each requirement to a story or project you can discuss.
272. Research the company's products, payment flows and recent engineering blog posts.
273. Prepare two or three questions per interviewer type (engineer, manager, staff, product).
274. Test your video setup, microphone and screen sharing the day before.
275. Keep a blank paper or digital whiteboard ready for design rounds.
276. Have water, and plan short breaks between rounds if the schedule allows.
277. Sleep well the night before; a rested brain beats one more hour of cramming.
278. Do a 20-minute warm-up on the day: one design pitch aloud, one coding pattern, one STAR story.
279. Review your 30-second answers for the topics you fear most.
280. Arrive (or log in) five minutes early and calm your breathing.
281. Read each question twice before answering; misreading costs more than a pause.
282. If you blank, restate the problem and start with what you know.
283. Write down the interviewer's constraints as they give them.
284. Manage time actively: note the start time and plan checkpoints.
285. If you realise a mistake, correct it openly; it shows rigour.
286. Don't compare rounds or dwell on a weak one; each round is scored independently.
287. Keep answers focused; long monologues lose interviewers.
288. Ask for clarification instead of guessing what the interviewer meant.
289. Show enthusiasm for the domain; fintech interviewers value people who care about money correctness.
290. Note down topics you struggled with after each round for later practice.
291. Send a short thank-you note if it's customary for the company.
292. Prepare your salary expectations and research the market range before the recruiter call.
293. Ask the recruiter about the loop format and which competencies each round assesses.
294. Prepare your own laptop environment for coding rounds: JDK, IDE settings, a scratch project.
295. Know how to run a quick JUnit test from the command line in case the environment is minimal.
296. Keep a one-page cheat sheet of your stories and key numbers, but don't read from it during rounds.
297. Breathe and slow down when nervous; speaking slowly sounds confident.
298. If a question is outside your experience, connect it to the closest thing you have done.
299. Finish strong: summarise, ask your question, thank them.
300. Afterwards, write a short reflection; every interview is practice for the next one.
## Recap

- Ten tips on one page are worth more than 150 read once.
- Habits come from saying them aloud in practice answers.
